# Fork release synchronization

Tags before v0.83.1 are unchanged upstream history. Stable tags from v0.83.1 onward are reconstructed from the exact upstream commit with `fork.patch`; new tags also snapshot the qualified candidate's release scripts, replay patch and caller/callee workflows. A release ledger committed on trusted fork main records each verified patched tag commit; it is pushed atomically with new tags and survives subsequent main changes. Recorded tags are never recreated or rewritten. For migration, unrecorded existing tags must match either the independently reconstructed legacy tree or the current trusted main snapshot; otherwise synchronization stops for manual review. Unsupported upstream tags or patch conflicts stop synchronization before any push. GitHub release descriptions retain upstream notes with a fork/history notice. Upstream release assets are not copied, and existing fork release assets require manual review.

Main synchronization merges the pinned upstream commit with current fork main using `git merge-tree --write-tree` (Git 2.38 or newer), then records both parents. It never replays the historical fork commit stack, rewrites fork history, or changes the checkout. Previously resolved upstream changes therefore remain integrated. The qualified fork application tree is authoritative: `fork.patch` is regenerated as its exact binary diff from the pinned upstream commit, excluding only `.github/scripts`, the sync/release workflows and the release ledger. New release trees use that frozen patch and automation snapshot before their identities are appended to the ledger; the ledger is not part of the patch or tag overlay. An empty application patch is valid and still receives the automation overlay. Existing recorded tags are validated without reconstruction and are never refreshed with a newer patch.

`bash .github/scripts/sync.sh verify` now qualifies upstream integration and patch freshness as well as tags. It never pushes, and fails if main or tags still need synchronization. A real overlapping change still stops before any ref update. Resolve that conflict once in an upstream merge on main, preserving both parents and the intended fork behavior, then rerun. Do not select an entire conflict side automatically. Merge-and-refresh reduces repeated historical conflicts; it cannot guarantee semantic compatibility with arbitrary future upstream changes.

Configure `FORK_SYNC_TOKEN` as a repository-scoped credential with Contents: write, Workflows: write, and Actions: write (for workflow dispatch). Branch/tag protection must permit its atomic pushes. Actions must be enabled and these workflow changes committed on the default branch before synchronization. The npm trusted publisher must identify this repository, caller `sync.yml`, and environment `release`; the package must permit trusted publishing under its 2FA policy. No npm token is used. The environment may require approval. Node 24 supplies a supported npm CLI. The repository and package must be public for npm provenance.

Hourly sync verifies/creates refs and GitHub releases, then dispatches `sync.yml` at the oldest unpublished patched tag. Both dispatch and publish independently fetch the ledger from origin/main and require the exact tag and commit to match; missing or malformed ledgers and mismatches stop the run. GitHub assigns the tag commit to `GITHUB_SHA`; the local reusable `release.yml` comes from that same commit, checks out and builds it, and publishes through OIDC with npm provenance. The publish job validates the tag, upstream parent, version and SHA. It serializes publishes, checks registry metadata afresh, never overwrites existing versions, and uses a version-specific dist-tag rather than rolling `latest` backwards. Stable releases can advance `latest` from a lower prerelease placeholder. Each successful run is picked up on the next hourly sync; failures are retried. GitHub Actions concurrency may replace a queued duplicate run, but later syncs retry pending versions. Manual registry writes outside this workflow can race its latest check and must be coordinated separately.

**Security boundary:** the dispatched tag supplies the workflow and publish script before those checks run. An attacker who can create or move an eligible tag can replace or bypass those checks; ledger validation in tag code is not an independent security boundary. Protect release tags against unauthorized creation, updates and deletion, protect main and its ledger and workflow changes, and tightly restrict the sync credential. Configure npm trusted publishing and the `release` environment (including any required reviewers and deployment restrictions) to authorize only intended releases. Verify the GitHub and npm OIDC workflow/environment configuration in the actual repository; this code cannot enforce those external settings. Protection must also account for changes between dispatch and execution.

If an already-existing unpublished patched tag lacks the workflow snapshot, truthful tag-ref dispatch is impossible without changing that immutable tag; automation stops and requires manual resolution rather than fabricating provenance. An already-published version must have the verified tag commit as `gitHead`; existing dist-tags are not reconciled. Registry or GitHub API outages, environment approvals, token permissions, disabled workflows, and npm trust/2FA configuration can block progress. Release reconciliation also stops on a missing upstream tag or existing fork release assets. No upstream binary asset is represented as patched.
